The pump inspection remains optional.” When a command is rejected, show: “No change was made. The destination is not confirmed; inspect the map report first.” These examples establish the right level of precision.

When an incident passes, do not say “area safe.” Say what is known: “No active spread is reported here. The crossing still needs inspection before travel.” Clear, factual text reduces false confidence and supports players who rely on text rather than animation.

### Field 09 expansion — workload growth plan

Test the authored catalog at 12, 30, 60, and 120 incident or recovery rows while keeping only a bounded active subset. Measure row validation at load, selection lookup, active list refresh, history open, and callback scheduling. The design should make it possible to add new content rows without editing each UI panel.

Measure closure ratio, evidence age, accepted/rejected orders, repeated warnings, work reassignment, and recovery completion. Do not optimize a high closure ratio by hiding uncertain reports or removing optional investigation. Performance and balance improvements must preserve the player’s ability to defer and review provenance.

### Field 10 expansion — approval-ready review set

The approval-ready set is one incident episode, one recovery episode, their data sheets, all text keys, story branch facts, owner dependency map, save behavior, UI state table, performance profile, and source-evidence checklist. It includes an exact review question for each unknown: does the fire owner already model this; can the map owner represent temporary closure; can the service owner accept this change; and can the journal persist this callback?

Rows with unanswered questions are marked conditional and are not included in a claimed implementation total. After approval, the first package stays deliberately small so the response contract can be exercised end to end before the rest of the atlas is filled.

## Pass 9 — Scenario run sheets and implementation review cases

### Field 01 expansion — example playthrough: the west crossing

The opening report says a returning delivery crew can see the crossing but has not tested it. The player can ask the crew for a second landmark, send a qualified inspector, or leave the route closed. If the player requests inspection, the map and expedition owners must confirm that the visit can be attempted. The story does not promise that the crossing will reopen.

After the inspection, the player receives one of three results: safe under a stated limit; restricted pending a repair; or no confirmed fault. A later delivery can test whether the current access rule is understood. If the driver arrives with an incompatible load, the crossing remains unchanged and the delivery can be redirected through an accepted route. The player can then accept a repair proposal, choose an alternate route, or defer the work. Closeout cites the inspection and route receipts, and the journal records the actual promise made to the delivery crew.

### Field 02 expansion — explicit input and output inventory

For the west-crossing sequence, the incident proposal reads the report source, known location reference, current route state, eligible inspector query, and weather observation if a current owner provides one. It may issue only an inspection request, route request, or project proposal supported by existing APIs. Its outputs are an evidence receipt, possible route-owner result, project link if accepted, and a callback eligibility fact. It does not write a route status, worker location, damage value, or delivery outcome directly.

This inventory should be repeated for every incident template and reviewed alongside current source. Proposed state fields are not accepted by virtue of appearing in a plan.

### Field 03 expansion — additional crossing episode rows

| Candidate record | Entry observation | Player action | Owner result |
|---|---|---|---|
| west_crossing_load_note | A cargo list exceeds the posted limit | Check the load or use another route | Expedition/access response |
| west_crossing_old_mark | Old warning is partly illegible | Find a dated notice source | Map/notice correction |
| west_crossing_inspector_wait | Inspector has not arrived | Reschedule or hold the site | Duty/expedition result |
| west_crossing_second_span | Report refers to a neighboring span | Confirm location before dispatch | Canonical site reference |
| west_crossing_detour_cost | Alternate route has a longer journey | Compare travel windows | Expedition estimate |
| west_crossing_first_use | Bridge owner reports a limit | Observe one accepted crossing | Route-owner status |
| west_crossing_material_return | Work is canceled after reservation | Return accepted materials | Inventory receipt |
| west_crossing_public_dispute | Residents question the restriction | Request another inspection or explain | Access/quest result |

### Field 04 expansion — dialogue keys and branch facts

Create dialogue keys for report arrival, first inspection, confirmed limit, rejected inspection, crew withdrawal, alternate route, material cancellation, first use, public disagreement, and unresolved closeout. Each key accepts only facts that the corresponding scene can know. A driver can report that a load was turned back but cannot know whether a support beam is structurally sound. An inspector can report the inspection result but cannot promise that every future load is safe.

The branch facts are inspection accepted; access limit accepted; delivery rerouted; materials returned; notice corrected; and public dispute open. These facts must belong to existing quest/history ownership if persistent. If the current quest system cannot record one safely, keep the corresponding scene conditional.

### Field 05 expansion — return-visit quest mini-chain

The return chain is: find the current notice; ask the next driver whether it was readable; compare the driver’s load to the posted limit; record a successful or rejected crossing through the route owner; report an unreadable notice; request correction; return after correction; close the work task with the actual service result. The player may stop after any step. No step assumes that the previous driver obeyed the sign.

Optional branches include helping a worker carry accepted tools, locating the original inspection note, and asking a nearby group whether the detour is usable. Each branch adds a source or service fact rather than generic experience points.

### Field 06 expansion — implementation case review

The reviewer traces five cases: valid inspection; denied access; no inspector available; project canceled after reservation; and load exceeds accepted limit. For each case, record state before command, accepted owner call, returned receipt, UI text, save point, and resulting map or service view. A rejected request must preserve existing truth. A replay after load must not repeat the inspection, item return, or route update.

### Field 07 expansion — visual states for route impact

Use separate line styles for known route, reported obstruction, owner-confirmed restriction, proposed detour, and inspected reopening. Each line has a text label and source. When two incidents affect the same route, show both references in the detail view and avoid picking an arbitrary winner. The map remains navigable if the player hides the incident overlay.

### Field 08 expansion — accessible notice and route copy

The sign and interface share the same short language: what is restricted, what load or travel condition applies, when it was checked, and where to ask for another inspection. Avoid abbreviations that only fit an icon. Support larger text and controller focus without losing the full route name.

### Field 09 expansion — exact profile data

The west-crossing test profile varies report age, inspector availability, route alternative, load class if supported, and weather observation. Keep each input fixed per seed. Measure action availability, rejected-command rate, owner-query count, save size, and time from inspection receipt to visible route update.

### Field 10 expansion — content gate

The crossing episode is ready only when every branch has an owner result and a readable explanation. If inspection results do not map to a current access API, the story remains an inspection quest without a reopening promise. This gives the plan a safe content-only version while the shared route contract is reviewed.

## Pass 10 — Campaign integration dossier and field review detail

### Field 01 expansion — incident continuity

An incident is resumed from its last accepted receipt and current owner facts. The active board summarizes current conditions; the journal preserves why the player made earlier decisions. A saved incident cannot freeze the weather, route, or service owners while the rest of the campaign advances. On return, the report identifies which facts changed while the player was away.

### Field 02 expansion — crew and duty edge cases

Before assigning a crew, check current availability, fitness, skill eligibility, and conflicting duty through their owners. If one member becomes unavailable before departure, the player can replace them or cancel. If availability changes while the crew is away, the response follows current expedition rules and reports what happened; the incident plan cannot teleport the worker home.

### Field 03 expansion — result card rows

| Result | Source | Visible next choice |
|---|---|---|
| Report corrected | Original reporter or second source | Close or inspect |
| Site inaccessible | Access/route owner | Wait or reroute |
| Service protected | Service owner receipt | Inspect or continue |
| Crew returned | Expedition arrival receipt | Reassign or rest |
| Work rejected | Inspector/service receipt | Rework or close |
| Recovery accepted | Current site owner | Reopen or retain limit |

### Field 04 expansion — story memory boundaries

The season records that an agreement was offered, accepted, refused, or not reached. It does not infer reconciliation from a later friendly conversation. Characters can remember the actual notice, inspection, or transfer that affected them. This gives callbacks continuity without a new global trust score.

### Field 05 expansion — cleanup and return tasks

Use small follow-ups to return borrowed tools, correct a stale marker, report that no fault was found, deliver a delayed inspection note, retrieve accepted surplus, and check a posted restriction after first use. Each task closes with an owner receipt or remains explicitly open.

### Field 06 expansion — evidence freshness

Every observation displays its source date and scope. An old observation can remain valuable history but cannot silently replace current owner state. If new evidence conflicts with a saved decision, open a new review task rather than mutating the old incident receipt.

### Field 07 expansion — resume behavior

On campaign resume, the incident board refreshes current owners once, identifies newly received results, and keeps prior selection when possible. A missing site reference is reported as stale content with a safe link to history; the panel does not crash or fabricate a map marker.

### Field 08 expansion — concise result wording

Prefer “Inspection received; route remains restricted” to “Area secured.” Prefer “No active spread reported” to “Fire defeated.” Result language names the evidence and the remaining limit. This is both more accurate and more useful for the next decision.

### Field 09 expansion — long-session check

Run the design review across a short session, a save/load break, and a long campaign with several closed incidents. Confirm callback one-shot behavior, history readability, and that the current map reflects owner state rather than the first report.

### Field 10 expansion — implementation handoff checklist

The foreman handoff names the package owner, exact changed paths, current owner calls, save contract, accepted episode rows, rejected rows, focused coverage, performance observation, and unresolved decisions. Content totals exclude draft or blocked rows so the plan cannot imply more playable material than the game actually exposes.

## Pass 11 — Wildland season workbook, incident evidence, and recovery service catalogue

This pass deepens the same ten fields. It does not create a new hazard authority, fire simulation, responder roster, damage ledger, map graph, or save section. Every incident below is a candidate content package whose entry conditions and consequences must be translated through the current owner contracts after a premise check. Fictional names are working labels. Any value that appears to be a threshold is illustrative until the authoritative system supplies a supported range. An authored report can describe a witnessed condition; it cannot silently mutate a simulation value.

### Field 01 expansion — a season should leave legible, bounded memories

Treat a season as a sequence of separate incidents connected by people, places, and repair work. The player should be able to explain why a situation changed from yesterday, which action affected it, and what uncertainty remains. The incident log therefore needs three distinct layers: observed facts, decisions taken, and later interpretation. A radio caller may report smoke beyond a ridge; the map should preserve that as an unconfirmed observation until a current map or incident owner confirms location. After confirmation, the original report remains in the history as the first signal, not as a second fire.

The season workbook uses a stable, human-readable incident key, an authored scenario reference, a location reference, a start and end condition, and a set of event references emitted by existing owners. Runtime identity, if needed, comes from the owning simulation. Content keys are not substitutes for save IDs. A record may be disabled independently if its location, interaction, or result consumer is unavailable. A disabled record must not change the season calendar, resource state, or story flags.

The play rhythm is split into actionable windows rather than continuous urgent notifications. A preparation window establishes what is known, what is not known, and what deadline is real. A response window exposes only actions supported by existing systems. A watch window allows the player to monitor changes without repeated modal interruption. A recovery window turns the incident into inspectable repair and return work. Every transition needs a clear reason and a visible receipt in the incident history.

### Field 02 expansion — evidence vocabulary and incident lifecycle

Use a small authored vocabulary to keep reports consistent across the map, journal, radio, and debrief. Candidate evidence states are: reported, corroborated, contradicted, outdated, resolved, and unresolved. These are presentation labels, not a new world-state enum. If the current journal already uses an equivalent status, map to that value rather than creating a second vocabulary. A report can be accurate about its source and still be wrong about the underlying event.

Lifecycle review questions:

1. What owner produced the fact, and at what simulation step?
2. Is the fact a direct observation, an authored claim, a player choice, or an inference?
3. Can the player revisit the source of the fact?
4. Does a later correction preserve the earlier report?
5. Can a save taken between receipt and verification resume without replaying a reward or losing the uncertainty marker?
6. Does a terminal incident state make cleanup visible without implying all consequences have ended?
7. Does the debrief distinguish absence of evidence from evidence that a threat has ended?

Candidate lifecycle row: a lookout hears a low aircraft-like sound during heavy wind. The report is tagged as an unconfirmed sound observation. A later sound-ranging result may corroborate or reject it if that system emits a matching observation. If no owner can evaluate the report, the narrative ends with uncertainty; the incident must not spawn a hostile unit or grant detection progress. This example deliberately tests content boundaries as well as tone.

Candidate lifecycle row: a crew reports that a cleared footpath has reopened after ash fall. The site card records the report and its source. The path remains available only if the current travel or map owner confirms availability. If it does not, the report can offer a follow-up inspection task but cannot promise route access.

### Field 03 expansion — candidate incident service cards

The following cards provide concrete authoring volume. Each is a separate possible situation, not a guaranteed runtime event. Entry conditions should name existing facts and never rely on prose-only flags.

| Working card | Site and first signal | Player-facing problem | Follow-up evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| North Orchard Smoke | Orchard edge; distant haze reported at dusk | Determine whether the smoke is from a controlled burn, a hot ash pocket, or an active incident | A dated lookout note and a later site inspection can resolve the source |
| Culvert Watch | Roadside drainage crossing; warm air and a brittle warning board | Keep the crossing under observation while checking the route owner’s condition | A route report distinguishes “inspect” from “passable” |
| Silted Pump Yard | Low field near a pump shed; water flow is slower after the incident | Recover access to a needed service without claiming a new water model | A maintenance receipt identifies the obstruction and current repair owner |
| Windbreak Rows | Shelter belt; damaged branches and dry debris reported | Decide whether to request cleanup or preserve the remaining cover | A later visit records labor used and whether the current site state changed |
| Old Quarry Turn | Exposed bend; ash obscures tracks on the approach | Verify route information before committing a crew | A map note can remain uncertain if no current travel owner can confirm |
| The Bell Shed | Volunteer store; warning bell is damaged, but the signal route is intact | Restore a trusted communication point using an existing repair interaction | A returned message confirms only the channel that was actually repaired |
| East Gate Families | Temporary gathering point; household count arrives through a witness | Establish contact and record needs through existing cohort or journal seams | A follow-up list separates confirmed names from unverified headcount |
| Dry Creek Nursery | Replanting beds; seed trays are usable but the water source is disputed | Coordinate inspection and water access without adding a parallel water reserve | The task closes only on a canonical water or site receipt |
| Burnt Signpost | Trail junction; old marker conflicts with a new map note | Correct the public information and retain the correction history | The map shows the corrected reference and the superseded warning |
| Watch Hut Window | Observation shelter; scratched lens and a partial log | Recover the previous shift’s notes and decide what warrants another watch | The player gets a source-labeled observation, not hidden certainty |
| Ash-Roof School | Disused school used as a meeting point; damaged roof is reported | Move a meeting or arrange a supported repair through current shelter/site owners | The meeting location changes only after a supported interaction |
| Borrowed Ladders | Work crew reports missing ladders after a roof inspection | Resolve custody and return without converting the incident into a generic theft plot | A signed handoff or inventory result closes the question |
| Ridge Radio Gap | Two outposts fail to exchange a scheduled check-in | Choose a relay visit or record the missed signal as unresolved | A radio owner result determines communication restoration |
| Meltwater Markers | A seasonal marker is displaced after runoff | Re-establish a locally understood reference point | A journal record preserves who moved it and why |
| The Quiet Fence | A repaired boundary has no new damage, but neighbors disagree about access | Mediate a documented access discussion and preserve the unresolved objection | The task may close with disagreement recorded rather than forced consensus |

The cards deliberately vary in certainty, scale, and closure. None awards a hidden score for a “correct” moral choice. Each has at least one result that preserves a cost or unresolved concern. The first content slice should select only cards whose owner seams can be demonstrated in current source and data.

### Field 04 expansion — three linked story strands

**The shared map.** A local cartographer has kept several versions of a hand-drawn route map. The first episode asks the player to retrieve the older copy from a flooded cabinet. The second compares its crossing notes against current route evidence. The third asks whether to publish a revised map with a caution marker or hold the map until another visit can verify the route. The consequence is informational: the journal records which revision was shared, which uncertainty remains, and who objected. It does not unlock a route unless the travel owner supports that route.

**The school roof.** A former teacher wants the damaged meeting hall repaired before the first cold rain. A carpenter believes the available salvage is insufficient, while a parent wants the meeting moved now. The opening task is a short inspection and a household notice. The middle task exposes two viable plans: move gatherings to an existing supported site, or schedule a repair only if materials and labor are actually available. A return scene shows the choice’s practical result. If the repair path is unavailable, the story still resolves through a clear relocation, preserving the school as a place people may revisit.

**The late check-in.** A volunteer relay operator misses two expected calls and leaves an apologetic note rather than a mystery threat. The player can visit the relay point, ask a neighboring group to carry a message, or wait for the next scheduled contact if the current radio owner supports it. A side path reveals the operator is caring for an injured sibling, without assigning a diagnosis or inventing a medical mechanic. Resolution requires an actual delivered message receipt. The story centers mutual aid and delayed information, not an ambush.

Each strand has a beginning, a middle decision, a return scene, and a closure record. A branch may vary the order of scenes, whether the player visited a site, and which supported action occurred. Branches should converge on a clear human consequence while keeping materially different outcomes visible.

### Field 05 expansion — field tasks with observable receipts

For each accepted task, author a bounded task record containing: working ID, title, source character or source system, available evidence, player action, precondition owner, completion owner, completion receipt, optional outcome, failure explanation, and revisit behavior. Do not add direct resource quantities until a current system can quote or consume them.

Candidate tasks:

- Verify the orchard smoke with a second observation and file the result.
- Deliver an updated warning to the culvert crew and record receipt.
- Inspect the pump yard with its caretaker; leave the water state to its owner.
- Move a public meeting from the damaged school to an available supported location.
- Return borrowed ladders and record both custodian names.
- Compare two map revisions and publish the uncertainty note.
- Ask the relay operator to choose a reliable check-in time.
- Gather the missing shift log from the watch hut.
- Post a translated or pictorial route notice when the supported UI/data path exists.
- Escort a worker to a safe meeting point using a currently available travel route.
- Revisit the nursery after an existing water delivery or site event.
- Interview two witnesses separately and preserve disagreement in the journal.
- Replace a physical sign through the current item or construction interaction.
- Record an inaccessible route and offer a later revisit task.
- Close a report as unresolved with an explicit reason and a source.
- Reopen the debrief when a genuinely newer owner event arrives.
- Compare a warning’s age with the current incident record before reusing it.
- Collect a maintenance handoff note and present it to the named successor.
- Notify households that the previous meeting location is unavailable.
- Record the return of a borrowed object as a custody fact, not a reward.

Each task’s outcome is narrative plus an owner receipt. Narrative completion alone must not be treated as operational completion. If a suitable receipt is unavailable, mark the task draft and author only the source dialogue and player-facing explanation.

### Field 06 expansion — evidence pack for closing a gap

A gap-seal review is a small dossier rather than a conclusion inferred from a plan title. It includes: the current public owner, all known producers and consumers, a reproduction path or proof of absence, the current save section if stateful, the content catalog schema and validator, a route from player input to domain call, and the result visible to the player. A reviewer classifies the package as content-only, presentation-only, or system-dependent. System-dependent rows remain blocked until a named integrator accepts the authority and claim.

The proposed plan-to-owner map must be a premise table. Candidate domains include map and travel, journal and chronology, radio and message delivery, cohorts and relationships, site construction, water service, inventory, and incident simulation. These are search directions only. During implementation, use exact current class and catalog names from source, not the provisional wording here. Plans already sealed in the live integration ledger stay sealed unless fresh evidence proves a new defect. No row in this pass reopens known debt by implication.

### Field 07 expansion — incident board interaction contract

The incident board has four reading surfaces: active, waiting on confirmation, recovery, and history. A single incident appears in only one active surface at a time. The card includes its current source, last update, information confidence, location evidence, available action, and the effect of selecting that action. “Waiting” means the player has an explicit next step or a stated reason to wait. It must not be a disguised dead end.

Opening a card does not advance time. Accepting an owner-supported command has an explicit confirmation only when the action is costly, irreversible, or changes a public commitment. A benign inspection request should not be hidden behind a warning modal. If an action becomes unavailable between preview and commit, the card refreshes with a reason and keeps the current selection. Closing the board restores focus to the control that opened it. Controller navigation reaches the same actions in the same order.

The map pin uses both a shape and a label to communicate status, so color is supplementary. A location that is approximate must visibly say “reported near” rather than appearing as a precise marker. The journal receipt provides a direct route back to the source card. An incident resolved on another screen updates the board without duplicate sound or repeated focus theft.

### Field 08 expansion — clear language for uncertainty and difficult outcomes

Use direct, calm wording that states who knows what. Examples for future copywriters:

- “The lookout reported smoke north of the orchard. The source is not confirmed.”
- “The map still marks the crossing as unverified.”
- “The crew returned the ladders. The handoff record names both custodians.”
- “The relay operator missed two calls. No cause has been confirmed.”
- “The meeting moved to the lower hall. The school roof remains unrepaired.”
- “The report is closed as unresolved. The last witness could not be reached.”

Avoid disaster spectacle, real-world agency names, and synthetic urgency. Copy does not call an outcome “safe” when only one specific hazard has been checked. Accessibility review includes persistent non-color status, adjustable text scale within current UI support, focus-visible state, concise screen-reader label order if a supported accessibility path exists, and optional reduced-motion behavior through current preferences. These are acceptance questions to verify, not claims that those capabilities already exist.

### Field 09 expansion — content and runtime envelope

Separate content volume from runtime cost. A draft library can contain many authored cards, but only the currently available subset should be loaded into a visible screen. Scenario selection should use catalog indexes or existing cached lookup paths. Do not create a permanent mirrored incident list if the owning domain can answer the current query. Update the board on actual events or bounded refresh points rather than polling every visible control each frame.

Candidate stress profiles for later owner review:

- A quiet session with one unresolved observation, one open side task, and an empty recovery queue.
- A busy session with several reports, multiple source systems, and one newly contradicted fact.
- A resumed session saved after a task preview but before its command commits.
- A long archive with repeated site visits and many superseded warnings.
- A content-disabled case where one incident’s route owner is missing.
- A low-resolution and controller-only navigation pass over the full board.

Measure visible card count, catalog load time, journal growth, allocations during refresh, and time to focus the first actionable control. Record the test environment when measurements become real. Until measured, any target is a proposed budget rather than verified performance.

### Field 10 expansion — first shippable slice and review gate

The first slice should contain one complete incident card, one linked character strand, one optional field task, one unresolved-information example, a board view, one journal receipt, and a resume checkpoint. It is complete only when the same accepted command produces a durable observable result through the current owner. Do not create broad content volume to mask a missing route or save seam.

Review checklist:

- Does the incident use only current facts or explicitly label authored uncertainty?
- Is each player action a real command exposed by an existing owner?
- Is each result visible after leaving and returning to the relevant screen?
- Can a reviewer trace the data ID, validation rule, producer, consumer, save owner, and player receipt?
- Does every story branch remain understandable if a side task is skipped?
- Can a denied or unsupported command explain how to proceed?
- Are approximate locations represented honestly?
- Does the content avoid implying a resolution broader than the evidence?
- Are competing incidents distinguishable in title, source, and next action?
- Can the package be removed by disabling its content rows without leaving dangling references?

The package remains a draft until content integrity, current-owner reachability, save behavior, and UI lifecycle are demonstrated in a focused integration. Passing prose review does not pass integration.


## Pass 12 — Response table, return-visit deck, and player-visible proof

This pass turns the season workbook into a reviewable content production packet. It adds operational examples to all ten fields while preserving the boundary that current simulation owners, not narrative text, determine fire, weather, travel, water, health, inventory, and site outcomes.

### Field 01 expansion — three lengths of incident play

A short incident should ask for one inspection and show one useful result. A medium incident can require a report, a player decision, and a return visit. A long episode can connect multiple sites, but it must have a readable status at every stop. The episode card declares its intended length, required visits, optional visits, and the point where the player can safely leave and resume. “Long” means more consequential choices and follow-up, not more repetitive clicks.

A player-facing contract is attached to every length band. Short: “Check the report and record what you find.” Medium: “Compare the report with a second source and agree what the community should do next.” Long: “Coordinate the response, then return to check whether the public repair and notice still match the site.” The contract cannot promise results outside available mechanics.

### Field 02 expansion — response choice table

| Choice family | Precondition evidence | Owner command needed | Receipt to show | If unsupported |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Verify a report | Source and location are named | Current incident/map query | Confirmed, contradicted, or unresolved source | Keep the observation provisional |
| Inspect access | Current route and crew available | Travel/site inspect command | Owner-issued access result | Offer deferment and show missing source |
| Notify a group | Audience and channel chosen | Current radio/message route | Sent, queued, or failed result | Preserve a draft notice only |
| Request cleanup | Site and task scope accepted | Construction/maintenance action | Accepted work order or refusal | Show a proposal with no progress claim |
| Move a meeting | Alternate location validated | Existing site or event action | Updated meeting receipt | Keep the original and state why it cannot move |
| Return an item | Item and custodian identified | Canonical inventory transfer | Transfer result and custodian history | Keep the custody question open |
| Revisit a witness | Contact path still valid | Current relationship/quest route | Contact made or no contact | Do not invent a new dialogue state |
| Close an incident | Required owner states meet their contract | Existing incident closeout | Closure scope and remaining obligations | Keep the incident active or pending |

Choice previews show known costs and irreversible effects from the owner quote. The interface must not infer a cost from prose. If a quote changes before commit, refresh it and require a new decision only when the affected cost or commitment is material.

### Field 03 expansion — twelve small incident variations

| Episode variation | First clue | Midpoint development | Reviewable ending |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orchard Row Return | A marker is newly scorched | Caretaker identifies an old controlled-work note | Close with source and inspection date |
| Two Calls at Dusk | Two reports use the same location name | One caller corrects the direction | Retain both messages and link correction |
| The Cold Culvert | Crew delays a planned crossing check | Route owner reports that an inspection is still needed | Mark the crossing pending, not closed |
| Missing Pegs | Repair stakes are absent | A neighboring group borrowed them for another task | Record transfer only through inventory owner |
| The Unsent Notice | A warning is drafted but no channel is selected | The audience asks for a shorter notice | Show draft status until delivery receipt |
| The Second Shift | A new crew sees different conditions | Their observation predates the last site update | Compare times before changing status |
| The Garden Bench | A shared resting point needs repair | A resident offers a different site for meetings | Show alternate site only if current site data supports it |
| The Folded Map | A hand-drawn map contradicts the board | The author explains its older date | Archive the source and cite current map evidence |
| The Split Path | Two routes are reported from one sign | A travel query rejects one route | Preserve the rejected route as a historical report |
| The Supply Box | A box is found at the wrong site | Its label names the former custodian | Ask inventory owner before changing location |
| The Quiet Afternoon | No new reports arrive | A character wants to know whether no report means resolution | Show “no new report” separately from “confirmed resolved” |
| The Return Bell | A repaired bell works at the site | No remote receiver confirms it | Record local function only; leave network status open |

These episodes are compact additions to larger arcs. Each can enrich a scene or objective without introducing a separate incident manager.

### Field 04 expansion — season callback matrix

| Earlier action | Later callback | What may be claimed |
|---|---|---|
| Published a caution with uncertainty | A traveler brings a newer observation | The caution was seen only if the message owner confirms audience |
| Moved a meeting | A household asks where the old meeting is now held | The location changed only if the site/event owner accepted it |
| Returned a shared tool | A later crew signs it out | Custody has a new receipt, not a permanent guarantee |
| Deferred a route | A map owner changes the route status | The route may now be queried; prior delay remains recorded |
| Preserved a witness disagreement | One witness later changes their account | The new statement supplements the prior one |
| Requested a cleanup | Work crew reports a scope limit | Only accepted work is presented as completed |
| Held an inspection | A second source arrives | The incident reopens only under the existing incident contract |
| Left a message queued | A relay returns | Delivery is credited only on an owner receipt |

The callback engine is not a new engine. Story content queries current history through its existing owner and presents the latest relevant receipt.

### Field 05 expansion — sample return-visit mini-chain

**Task A: Find the source.** The player visits the watch hut and reads a partial shift log. The task can finish with a source record even if the smoke is not confirmed. **Task B: Compare the map.** The player submits the log’s direction to the current map or incident owner. A supported response may confirm, contradict, or leave it unresolved. **Task C: Choose an audience.** The player drafts a public notice based only on the result and selects a currently supported channel. **Task D: Revisit after a change.** A later owner event supplies a new observation, at which point the old notice can be reviewed. **Task E: Close with scope.** The player can state that the report is resolved, remains uncertain, or is superseded by new evidence. Only the owner’s actual result determines which labels are available.

Side branches include the watch keeper correcting their own note, a resident declining public naming, the channel refusing a notice that exceeds its supported length, and the map owner reporting that the location is too imprecise. None should cause a soft lock. Every branch has a readable next step or a deliberate terminal explanation.

### Field 06 expansion — review examples that reject false gap claims

A content row is not proof that a feature is missing. Suppose a planned public notice appears absent from one UI screen: first trace whether another panel already presents it; then check the data consumer and any recent integration package; then verify that the incident owner emits the relevant fact. If only the presentation is missing, route the finding to the current UI owner. Do not create a second notice system. If the producer is missing, document the exact event and ask the foreman to assign a narrow implementation package. If a current owner rejects the command, preserve the refusal as an evidence-backed limit.

A proposed cleanup task may seem unimplemented because a quest catalog has no row. Check the current construction and maintenance paths before declaring a gameplay gap. If a generic maintenance work order already exists, add authored content through that owner. If the data is present but unreachable, find the accepted route and leave the catalog unchanged until its current validator can prove the link.

### Field 07 expansion — incident detail wireframe in words

The first line is a concise status and source: “Reported near Orchard Row · lookout message · one day ago.” The next block says what is known and what is uncertain. An optional “History” disclosure shows previous and corrected reports. The action list contains only commands that the current owners have approved. Each action description names its direct effect. A right-side map preview is approximate when the evidence is approximate. The final strip shows last update and the path back to the journal entry.

When an incident has no available action, the empty state says why: “No confirming observation is available. You can return after a new map or lookout report.” It does not show an inactive generic button. A resolved incident can show open recovery work without returning to the active queue unless the owner’s lifecycle says it is reopened.

### Field 08 expansion — response text and interruption examples

A critical interruption should be reserved for a real owner-emitted urgent event. New reports with no action do not steal focus. The notification states the source and the one next action, if one exists. A text equivalent persists in the incident history. Repeat reports can coalesce only if the current notification owner supports it and the coalesced message preserves all sources.

Short copy samples: “New report: the culvert crew has not confirmed access.” “The route note is still unverified.” “The sign was changed; the map has not updated.” “No new lookout report arrived today.” “A second witness disagrees with the first direction.” “The cleanup request was declined because the site owner could not confirm access.” Text distinguishes time passing from urgency and does not assert imminent harm without a supported cause.

### Field 09 expansion — archive retention and query discipline

The incident history may become longer than an active board can render comfortably. Keep active state separate from immutable history only through current owners. A visible archive can filter by site, source, and status, but filtering is presentation-only. Search should be bounded and should not load all prose into a daily simulation tick. A stale report can be retained with its age; it need not be deleted to keep the board current.

The replay review compares a fresh run and a resumed run at the same simulation step: incident IDs, event order, notices delivered, quest receipts, and visible status. Any divergence is recorded against the owner path that produced it. Narrative variation uses stable choice sources. The implementation dossier measures archive size, loading time, panel refresh cost, and duplicate receipt count; the plan does not set fabricated pass numbers.

### Field 10 expansion — release-ready content inventory

A future content release inventory groups rows into: launch-critical, optional side task, callback-only, dependency-blocked, and retired. For each row, include the current validator result, reachability proof, first player-visible surface, exact owner receipt, save/reload behavior, and content reviewer. Exclude disabled drafts from playable volume totals.

The season is ready for a production decision when one complete short incident, one medium episode, and one later callback all use the same verified source/event chain without creating parallel state. The final handoff records which cards were accepted, which were deferred, the reason for each deferral, current owner names and paths, and any behavior that must remain unchanged. Until that evidence exists, every new card in this pass is a candidate rather than shipped content.


## Pass 13 — Season cast, scene fragments, and consequence-aware quest writing

This pass adds story-building material that can sit on top of the verified incident receipts. It is intentionally subordinate to field tasks and owner integration: dialogue may explain a result, but cannot generate one.

### Field 01 expansion — character continuity through changed responsibilities

Build the season cast around changing responsibilities rather than archetypes. Candidate roles include a lookout learning to mark uncertainty, a caretaker protecting a shared meeting place, a repair worker who wants a bounded scope, a map keeper whose notes are useful but old, a relay operator balancing private messages and public warnings, and a new volunteer who inherits incomplete records. A character card records what the person knows, what they personally observed, what they heard from someone else, what they want next, and which later event can change their view.

Continuity should survive player disagreement. A resident who opposed a closure can later cooperate with a repair without becoming an ally flag. A worker can accept a handoff while still disputing the public notice. The journal remembers concrete statements and actions. It does not flatten a complicated relationship into “likes player” or “trust +1” unless the existing relationship owner exposes that exact fact.

### Field 02 expansion — scene construction pattern

A scene card has a location, participants, triggering evidence, one immediate question, two or more player responses, current-owner action where needed, and a closing line that reflects the actual result. Dialogue choices divide into information gathering, commitment, refusal, and deferment. Information gathering must not secretly commit. Refusal has a clear reason and a way to revisit only when a new fact arrives. Deferment explains what will make the task actionable.

A consequence check follows each scene: which future line changes, which quest becomes available or closes, which owner receipt is referenced, what remains uncertain, and whether the scene can be repeated without duplicating an award. A writer may author several lines for one state, but a scene variation cannot claim a different simulation outcome without a different owner result.

### Field 03 expansion — side-quest story cards

| Working quest | Opening beat | Player contribution | Callback |
|---|---|---|---|
| A Line on the Map | A map keeper asks who last changed a trail note | Compare date and source with a current route query | Later travelers cite the correct revision |
| Bell Before Dusk | A caretaker wants the bell checked before a meeting | Request an owner-supported inspection and notify attendees | The caretaker notes whether the warning was heard |
| The Returned Hammer | A worker finds a tool with no custodian label | Trace inventory evidence and ask nearby crews | The owner records a return or keeps location unknown |
| Two Chairs Missing | A meeting organizer counts fewer seats than expected | Check the current storage owner and offer a supported alternative | A later gathering records its actual setup |
| The Quiet Errand | A resident asks for a private message | Confirm audience and use the current message path | The sender decides whether to share the reply |
| Shift Notes | A new volunteer inherits an undated notebook | Add provenance only through an approved journal/record path | The next shift leaves a dated note |
| Sign in the Rain | A public marker has faded | Verify the route before proposing a replacement | A later visit checks whether the sign remains legible |
| A Place to Wait | A traveler needs a sheltered meeting point | Locate an existing supported site and announce it | The traveler reports whether the site was reachable |
| One More Witness | Two reports disagree about direction | Invite a second witness without coercion | Agreement or disagreement is preserved |
| The Spare Blanket | A shared item is found at the wrong location | Use canonical inventory custody and return behavior | A future borrower signs it out |
| After the Notice | Residents saw different warning versions | Compare delivery receipts and publish a correction | The old version remains discoverable in history |
| A Better Handoff | Two shifts use different check-in habits | Let them choose a supported reminder or ledger path | The next handoff tests whether the choice helped |

These quests create varied authored outcomes without inventing reward currencies. Each requires a source, a real owner receipt if operational, and one human callback.

### Field 04 expansion — sample dialogue with state-sensitive endings

At the damaged sign, the map keeper says: “I drew this before the lower steps gave way. It still gets people to the mill. I cannot tell you whether it gets them back.” The player may ask when it was drawn, ask who has used it since, request a current route check, or leave it in place with its date visible. If the route owner confirms a path, the character replies: “Then add the date you checked. I want the old line kept beside it.” If the route remains unknown, the reply is: “Leave the question on the board. A blank space would look like an answer.” The dialogue does not set route state.

At the end of a returned-tool quest, the worker says: “It is back on the shelf. I still want the night crew to sign for it.” If inventory confirms the return, the journal says so. If the item was merely seen in the room but not transferred, the text says “found at the workshop” and leaves custody unresolved. This wording provides concrete writing guidance for truthful story callbacks.

### Field 05 expansion — sequel and consequence planning

A story sequel is available only from a meaningful changed fact: a new report, a completed repair, a delivered message, a returned item, or a changed request. It is not launched merely because time passed unless a current owner emits a time-based trigger. Sequel planning uses three columns: prior choice, current observable evidence, and next player action. If no evidence exists, write a reflective scene that does not claim a changed world.

Candidate sequel types include: a corrected record used by a new volunteer; a public notice that prompts an objection; a repair that proves narrower than expected; a private message whose sender chooses not to open a reply; a meeting moved to a reachable site; and a witness returning to correct their own account. Each should include an optional path that leaves the relationship unchanged.

### Field 06 expansion — story implementation handoff

A writer’s packet includes dialogue keys, speaker attribution, triggering receipts, allowed variables, all branch endings, unsupported-action fallback, and the precise visible surface for each callback. Before writing a conditional line, confirm that its condition exists in an existing owner or explicitly mark it as an authoring proposal. Writers do not invent a “fire resolved” or “resident trust” variable to make prose flow. The integrator maps accepted facts to existing IDs and requests a decision when the desired state has no owner.

### Field 07 expansion — journal and quest presentation

Quest text should show the next action, source, and optional status. A prose excerpt is not the only way to understand completion. The journal summary has a concise factual line followed by a character callback; the player can expand the source note. A quest that ends unresolved displays why and whether new evidence can reopen it. Reopening reuses its history and does not create a duplicate quest reward.

### Field 08 expansion — character voice and accessibility

Voice variation comes from diction, attention, and priorities rather than spelling quirks. A map keeper asks about dates and landmarks; a repair worker asks about scope and materials; a caretaker asks who will use the space; a relay operator asks who can hear a message. Keep each line readable aloud and avoid relying on visual punctuation alone to communicate uncertainty. Important source details appear in accessible text, not only voice audio. A muted-audio path preserves the same clue through captions or a journal note if those current surfaces support it.

### Field 09 expansion — narrative volume controls

Long campaign text loads only for the selected scene. Repeated ambient lines use a bounded rotation selected deterministically where replay matters. The same authored key should not be copied into multiple catalogs with divergent wording; use the existing localization/content authority. Archived scenes may remain visible in journal history without being loaded into the active incident board.

### Field 10 expansion — story acceptance

Story review asks whether each character wants something understandable, whether the player can refuse without being punished by hidden state, whether every callback cites a real event, and whether the ending accurately describes what remains. A scene is ready when copy, branch conditions, data references, and owner receipts agree. Narrative review alone cannot accept the quest as playable.


## Pass 14 — Worked season playthrough and integration evidence trace

This is a review walk-through, not a claim that the episode is present in the build. It connects the earlier incident, story, task, UI, save, and performance proposals into one player path.

### Field 01 expansion — day one: receive, verify, and choose

The day opens on a quiet board. A lookout reports smoke north of the orchard; the report is stamped with source and age, and its map pin says “reported near.” The player opens the detail card. The card separates the lookout’s observation from the current map result. No urgent alarm fires because the report is not yet confirmed and has no owner-emitted emergency status.

Three commands appear only if current owners support them: request a map check, visit the watch hut, or leave the report pending. The player selects the map check. The command preview shows the source and likely direct effect: ask for an updated route/location assessment. It does not promise that the route is safe. After confirmation, the owner returns “location uncertain.” The board retains the original report, records the new result, and does not change incident severity or fire state.

The player next visits the watch hut, reads a partial shift note, and compares the recorded direction. The journal source is accessible from the card, and closing the journal restores focus to the same report. The player can now record a corroborating observation, but the location remains approximate. A narrative line from the lookout says they will check the ridge at first light. That line creates a future intention only if an existing quest/event contract can represent it.

### Field 02 expansion — day one save boundary and result replay

Save immediately after the map query returns but before the player selects a follow-up. On reload, verify: the report ID is unchanged; the old observation remains; the uncertainty label persists; the map query is not repeated; no notification replays; the first available action remains the same; and the journal source link still opens the correct note. If the current save owner cannot represent a pending report plus its query receipt, do not claim this save boundary is supported; redesign the content slice to use the owner’s existing durable state.

A second save occurs after the player asks the lookout to return later. The quest receipt must appear once. Reload cannot spawn a duplicate visit or duplicate dialogue reward. If the narrative callback is not persisted by the owner, it should be a transient line rather than a promised recurring state.

### Field 03 expansion — day two: a route report and an unrelated repair

A new source reports that the culvert path may be open. This report is not automatically attached to the orchard incident. The board shows it as a separate item because location, source, and route status differ. The player can inspect the relation between the sites, but the story does not merge them just because both are in the same region.

A caretaker asks for a meeting move because the school roof inspection is pending. The player opens the site owner’s current status. If the meeting location is available, the supported event/site command can move it; if not, the task remains a clear proposal. The player chooses to notify attendees through an existing channel. The message preview names its audience. The delivery result is shown as sent, queued, or failed according to the communication owner. The incident board does not infer that everyone received it.

### Field 04 expansion — day three: receive correction and resolve scope

The lookout reports that the smoke was a controlled work signal on a neighboring plot. This message changes the interpretation, not necessarily the incident object’s underlying simulation state. The player sees both reports with source and age. If the current incident owner can resolve the incident with scope, it returns “report source identified; no active incident confirmed.” If that owner cannot, the plan keeps the story as an unresolved information thread rather than manufacturing a resolved flag.

The player then chooses what to tell the community. A concise notice states that the source was identified and that the orchard ridge itself was not inspected. The UI previews the wording and audience. A public correction does not erase the original report; the journal links the correction to the earlier claim. The lookout character admits they had turned toward the wrong ridge, while the map keeper asks that the original wording remain for context. This callback changes dialogue because a real correction receipt exists.

### Field 05 expansion — optional tasks and different endings

Optional task A lets the player ask the caretaker to verify the school meeting alternative. If the site owner confirms the lower hall, the event owner may accept the move. If it refuses, the story still finishes with a notice that the meeting is postponed. Optional task B returns a borrowed ladder through inventory. If the ladder was only seen in the workshop and no transfer was recorded, the task ends “location found; custody not confirmed.” Optional task C asks a second witness about the smoke source. If the witness disagrees, the incident record retains the disagreement rather than reopening the event automatically.

Three valid endings follow:

- Confirmed local source: the source was identified by owner-supported evidence, the notice was delivered, and the incident closes with the nearby area explicitly uninspected.
- Unresolved source: evidence conflicts or the owner cannot determine a source; the incident remains pending with a specific next evidence request.
- No new report: the player stops pursuing the optional return; the board says no new evidence arrived, without claiming that danger ended.

### Field 06 expansion — exact trace a future implementer must produce

A future handoff records the UI command name, current host handler, owning Core API, source event or receipt, catalog IDs, current save section if stateful, journal/report surface, and focused verification command. It also records the precise state that was intentionally not changed, such as route access, fire intensity, resource use, or resident relationship. “Connected” requires evidence for all relevant stages. A panel button and valid JSON row do not complete the trace.

The person reviewing the package tries one denied path and one owner failure. For example, the message channel rejects the public notice. The player receives a useful explanation; the incident remains unresolved, and no delivery receipt is added. This probe distinguishes a real end-to-end path from a happy-path-only content demonstration.

### Field 07 expansion — board transition transcript

Initial state: “Smoke report — reported near Orchard Row — from the north lookout — location unconfirmed.” After map query: “Location still uncertain — map service could not confirm the ridge.” After the shift note: “A second source points toward the orchard road; the exact source remains unverified.” After correction: “The lookout identified a neighboring work signal; the orchard ridge was not inspected.” After notice: “Correction queued for the public channel” or “Correction delivered,” as returned by the channel. After closeout: “This report is resolved as to its likely source; no inspection of the orchard ridge was recorded.”

Each line is composed from returned facts. Do not display all transitions simultaneously on the active board. The history view allows inspection of the complete trace.

### Field 08 expansion — emotional pacing and player agency

The episode allows the player to stop after the first report, leave uncertainty intact, and continue the wider campaign. The character callback rewards attention without unlocking a mandatory route. Time pressure exists only if a current owner or scenario clearly exposes a deadline. The player can read the source note later. Sound cues are tied to the notification owner, and the text history contains the same important information.

### Field 09 expansion — measurements during the worked run

For an implemented prototype, record the number of owner queries made from the incident detail, time to open the source note, board refresh duration after new evidence, total journal rows added, size of saved incident references, and duplicate notifications after reload. Repeat with several unrelated open tasks so the board does not hide them. Compare a normal interaction and a controller-only interaction. No metric is considered passing until an actual baseline and acceptable limit are approved.

### Field 10 expansion — worked-run acceptance decision

The run is accepted if all three endings are reachable through owner-supported facts, each result is accurately worded, branch callbacks cite the correct receipt, and a save/resume does not repeat or erase events. A denial and an invalid-location path remain understandable. The episode may be approved as a narrow playable slice even if optional tasks remain disabled. The handoff labels disabled content and current unknowns instead of counting every written task as released content.


## Pass 15 — Recovery stewardship, observation records, and closure follow-through

This pass shifts attention from the initial incident toward weeks of return visits. It proposes content for observation, repair handoff, and public understanding without adding ecological simulation rules or making authored claims about real-world fire behavior.

### Field 01 expansion — recovery should be visible in small changes

After the immediate report is settled, the player should see small, dated changes at familiar locations: a sign restored, a meeting moved back, a path inspection completed, a damaged storage area still closed, or a caretaker asking for another review. These changes create continuity without promising that every landscape condition evolves in a new simulation. The player’s recovery board identifies which changes are owner-confirmed and which are simply observations.

A recovery loop has four steps: revisit, compare, hand off, and return. Revisit uses a valid route. Compare places the current observation beside the previous one. Handoff sends the issue to the responsible owner or records that no owner accepted it. Return checks the later receipt. A single location may have several independent concerns, and clearing one must not close them all.

### Field 02 expansion — observation record fields

A candidate observation record describes: site; observed condition; observer; observation date or simulation step; method; prior related record; confidence language; owner query; result; follow-up owner; and whether the finding is public. An observation is not an environmental state mutation. A character can describe what they saw; the simulation owner decides what state changed.

The record distinguishes “not observed,” “not changed,” and “changed.” An empty field is not a negative result. If a player returns but cannot reach a location, the record says access was unavailable. If a route owner confirms a visit and the observer reports no visible change, the note says exactly that. A later observation appends to history rather than rewriting the earlier note.

### Field 03 expansion — recovery site cards

| Site | Return question | Useful player action | Bound closeout |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orchard edge | Was the warning marker replaced after the source was identified? | Query site/map owner and compare notice date | Marker current or still pending |
| Culvert crossing | Did inspection occur after the path report? | Request an owner-supported visit | Inspection receipt or deferred access |
| Pump yard | Did the repair owner respond to the maintenance note? | Present the existing work request | Accepted scope, refusal, or no response |
| School meeting room | Can the previous meeting return to its original location? | Query current site/event state | Confirmed move or continued alternate |
| Watch hut | Has the next shift added a dated observation? | Read the current log source | New note or no new entry |
| Shared tool store | Was the borrowed equipment returned? | Check canonical inventory custody | Transfer receipt or unknown location |
| Lower hall | Is the alternate meeting site still available? | Query the current site owner | Available or unavailable status |
| Nursery beds | Has the caretaker asked for another inspection? | Revisit only on current request | Request open or closed by its source |
| Trail marker | Does the sign match the map’s current source? | Compare current revisions | Correct, stale, or unverified |
| Relay shed | Is the check-in schedule still useful? | Ask operator and inspect current channel | Revised, declined, or pending schedule |
| Quarry road | Is the route still approximate or confirmed? | Query current travel owner | Route result without extrapolation |
| Shared well notice | Is the posted public instruction current? | Compare water/service owner result | Notice updated or left uncertain |

These cards keep recovery work tied to recurring places and distinguish one site’s many possible service owners.

### Field 04 expansion — aftercare story arc

**The marker keeper.** After a public notice changes, the marker keeper asks whether the old board should be taken down. The player checks whether the new notice was delivered and whether the route owner confirmed the information. If delivery remains pending, the keeper can leave both versions with dates. If the route is confirmed, the old caution can be archived without erasing its history. The keeper later teaches another volunteer how to mark a source date.

**The nursery caretaker.** The caretaker does not ask the player to make the beds productive. They ask for help establishing who will inspect the water connection and when the next visit can occur. The player queries the current service owner, records the accepted maintenance contact, and returns after a supported delivery or owner event. If no such event exists, the story closes with a clear reminder that service remains unconfirmed.

**The crew that did not return.** A crew accepted a small maintenance task but did not file a completion receipt. The player checks its last known handoff, contacts the crew through an existing route if available, or leaves the project pending. A later explanation might be that the crew was reassigned, but only a real roster/task receipt can say so. The arc explores how communities report incomplete work without accusing people based on absence alone.

### Field 05 expansion — recovery quests

- Revisit a notice and compare its effective date to the latest owner result.
- Ask the marker keeper whether an outdated board has been removed.
- Carry a maintenance request to its current site owner.
- Record a crew’s refusal or inability to accept additional work.
- Confirm the alternate meeting place remains available.
- Ask the caretaker which follow-up they want, if any.
- Check whether inventory recorded the borrowed item’s return.
- Compare two dated observations without calculating an unsupported trend.
- Notify affected residents when an accepted schedule changes.
- Close a report only to the scope confirmed by its owner.
- Ask a witness whether their previous statement still stands.
- Reopen a location card when a new source arrives.
- Mark an observation as inaccessible when the route was refused.
- Retrieve the prior notice and link it to the correction.
- Record a public thank-you without implying a mechanical reward.
- Ask the next shift to attach a source and date to its note.

### Field 06 expansion — recovery owner map

Each aftercare task maps to one primary owner and, where needed, one notification owner. The map records query, command, event/result, save path, and presentation. A follow-up that spans several owners is decomposed into separate tasks with explicit handoff. A story callback may reference a previous owner result but cannot carry it into a second mutable copy.

### Field 07 expansion — history and return controls

The recovery view groups sites by new evidence, accepted work, pending owner response, and no recent update. It does not infer “stalled” from elapsed time unless the owner provides a deadline. A return action opens the source note and lets the player ask for a current owner query. The history view shows the full chain and the player can compare two records side by side.

### Field 08 expansion — closure wording

- “The marker was checked today. Its wording matches the current route note.”
- “The site could not be reached; no inspection occurred.”
- “The maintenance owner accepted the request. Work has not started.”
- “The alternate room remains in use because reopening was not confirmed.”
- “No new report arrived. The previous uncertainty remains.”
- “The item was seen at the store; custody was not transferred.”
- “The crew has not returned a completion receipt.”
- “The observation was closed as inaccessible, not resolved.”

These lines prevent a quiet board or a missed visit from becoming a false all-clear.

### Field 09 expansion — archive and comparison workload

The archive retains related observation IDs but renders summaries incrementally. Comparing two records reads their source values without generating a new observation. A return visit does not reprocess every old quest. Performance review records archive query cost, visible card count, source-note load, and refresh response after new evidence. Any derived comparison cache is disposable and not part of gameplay save state.

### Field 10 expansion — recovery closure dossier

The closure dossier includes last confirmed state, latest observation, owner response, unresolved concerns, public message receipts, and next responsible party. If the next party has not accepted responsibility, say so. A location can be marked complete for one work scope while retaining a different recovery task. The final review samples one confirmed correction, one owner refusal, one inaccessible site, and one report with no new evidence.


## Pass 16 — Incident authoring acceptance examples

This closing tranche adds compact examples to help the authoring and integration review distinguish a complete incident from a convincing but unsupported story.

### Fields 01–03 — report cards with bounded claims

| Report | Exact known fact | Claim deliberately withheld | Useful player action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm gate latch | A caretaker felt warmth at the outside handle | No claim about what is behind the gate | Ask for the current site owner’s inspection |
| Bent marker post | A post is leaning beside a trail | No claim that the trail is blocked | Query route status and record location |
| Unlit signal window | One lookout saw no light at a scheduled time | No claim that the relay is broken | Check for a later communication receipt |
| Damp store ledger | The paper record is wet and partly unreadable | No claim that stored goods are damaged | Ask inventory owner for current stock |
| Quiet pump shed | No worker answered during one visit | No claim about staffing or pump operation | Leave an authorized message or return later |
| Split ash line | Two witnesses describe different directions | No claim that one witness is lying | Preserve both reports and seek new evidence |
| Old meeting notice | The notice has an expired date | No claim that the meeting is canceled | Query event/site owner and publish a correction |
| Missing return mark | No sign-out sheet shows an item returned | No claim that the item is lost | Query canonical inventory and contact custodian |

An authoring reviewer should be able to underline the exact evidence for each sentence in a card. Any sentence without a source is rewritten as a question, a character belief, or removed.

### Fields 04–05 — consequence and closure variants

For each report, prepare one confirmed result, one contradicted result, one unavailable-owner result, and one no-new-evidence result where the current owner supports those distinctions. The player’s story outcome can be:

- Confirmed: the source or owner result supports the reported fact.
- Narrowed: one part is confirmed, while a second part remains uninspected.
- Contradicted: the owner returns a conflicting result with its own source.
- Deferred: an action cannot occur because a named precondition is absent.
- Unresolved: no valid new evidence is available.
- Withdrawn: the request source cancels it.
- Superseded: a newer owner receipt replaces the current operational instruction while preserving history.

Do not enable a result label merely because it makes a scene easier to write. The owning contract determines whether the branch is legal.

### Fields 06–10 — integration review prompts

A second reviewer checks that one report can be created, opened, sourced, acted on, closed, and revisited through current owner paths. The review also asks whether content disablement leaves no orphan objectives, whether a failure can be retried without duplicate effects, whether status survives the supported save boundary, and whether the interface distinguishes uncertain locations and stale facts.

The final package includes a discrepancy list between authored intent and current API. Each mismatch is resolved by changing the content, obtaining an accepted owner extension, or marking the row blocked. No mismatch is papered over by a new local boolean. The incident is counted as playable only after the same result appears consistently in board, journal, and saved campaign history.


## Pass 17 — One incident content record, fully annotated

A candidate record called “Orchard Row, First Report” illustrates how the narrative and system boundary can be written together. Its working key is provisional and must be replaced or accepted by the current content owner. The summary says a lookout reported smoke near an orchard at dusk. The source is a lookout message; the location is approximate; the report is not an owner-confirmed incident. The opening objective is to review the report and choose whether to request verification, visit the source, or wait.

Its required references are the current lookout source, the map location if valid, the incident/journal surface, and any accepted quest command. Its optional references are a follow-up message and a return visit. If a route or message owner is missing, the optional branch is disabled; if the core report cannot be queried or recorded, the entire record remains draft. The card cannot directly alter fire intensity, weather, travel state, water stock, or damage.

The first receipt links the report to its author and arrival step. A second receipt, if the map owner returns a result, links to the query and records confirmed, contradicted, or uncertain only where those outcomes exist. If the player waits, the objective can remain open without running an unbounded timer. A later report reuses the original source history and does not create a duplicate incident unless the current owner declares a new event.

The story has four short lines: the lookout reports what they saw; a map keeper asks for the source’s age; a caretaker asks whether the public meeting should move; and the lookout later corrects the direction if the owner-supported evidence warrants it. The correction does not imply the orchard was inspected. Optional quests cover comparing a dated map, returning a borrowed ladder, and notifying the meeting group. Each task names its owner receipt.

The UI states are draft report, actionable report, waiting for evidence, result received, and closed within scope. The screen shows source, time, approximate location, known facts, unknown facts, action, and latest owner result. It does not show a danger score without an authoritative value. The accessibility review checks that “approximate” is read in text and not color alone, the map pin has a distinct uncertain marker, the journal can be reached with controller input, and closing the detail returns to its list row.

A saved run captures only state through the current incident, quest, journal, or campaign owners. The review tests before query, after query, before notice, after notice, and after closure. It checks duplicate messages and receipts, missing catalog references, and removal of the optional branch. Performance review measures opening the board and loading its source note with a representative active history. The release note reports the exact playable scope: report intake and verification only if both owners agree, with meeting notice and ladder return listed separately if enabled.

The authoring card is rejected if it claims “fire contained” from a source-only report, if it creates a new incident flag inside the panel, if it duplicates an existing content record, or if it has no player-visible result. It is accepted for implementation only after the owner, validator, save path, and UI route are named in the package handoff.


The post-incident board also needs a distinction between a site observation and a forecast. An observer may say that dry debris is visible; the plan cannot infer how quickly it will ignite or whether it increases a fire’s spread. If a future fire simulation exposes an authored weather or fuel query, the incident can display that result with a source and time. Until then, keep such prose descriptive and avoid numeric danger bands. A recovery objective may request that the current maintenance owner clear a site, but it cannot make a promised prevention claim. A useful review asks the player what changed, what evidence supports the change, and what remains outside the inspected boundary. If the answer is only “the map turned green,” the feedback is too broad. This check protects both narrative trust and the simulation’s ownership boundary.

Before any future incident is released, compare its player-facing location wording against the map owner’s precision. A named ridge may be an authored landmark, while the current map result is only a nearby sector. The incident card should not create a more precise pin than the source supplies. If a later observation narrows the location, retain the first approximate report and display the newer result separately. This keeps the chronology useful for review and avoids rewriting what the lookout originally knew. The same rule applies to wind direction, visibility, and site access: show only values returned through a current owner contract, label their age, and avoid projecting them forward into an unverified forecast.

## Pass 18 — Current owner collision map and recovery-specific expansion route

This pass revises the expansion route against current integrated evidence. Plan names below are repository-local identifiers. The older Plans 162–165 reconnaissance document explicitly warns that its numbering is external and conflicts with repository numbering; use system names and live ledger status as the authority.

### Field 01 expansion — distinguish shelter fire from outdoor fire
