## Pass 57 — Recovery state transitions and evidence-driven scenario ladders

This pass defines a reusable state ladder for burn-recovery work. It is a content and routing contract over existing disaster, weather, expedition, cartography, inventory, survivor, archive, and vehicle owners. The ladder is deliberately narrower than a fire simulator: it tracks the player’s recovery case, not a new physical hazard model.

### Field 01 expansion — Reported state

A case begins when an owner or witness reports a route, structure, cache, water point, or memorial concern. The record carries source, time, location, confidence, and privacy scope. Reported does not unlock a dangerous action. It offers verification, a safe delay, a map note, or an owner query.

### Field 02 expansion — Verification state

Verification requests an owner-supported observation: route survey, weather refresh, inventory inspection, air or water sample, structure measurement, communications check, or witness confirmation. The request has one owner, one expected receipt, a timeout, and a fallback. Recovery does not mark a report verified from a second copy of the same report.

### Field 03 expansion — Prepared state

When evidence supports a low-risk operation, the case enters prepared state. The player sees required crew, equipment, route window, consent, and return condition. Vehicle and expedition owners decide whether the package can depart. A prepared case can be paused without losing the verified evidence.

### Field 04 expansion — Active field state

An active field case has a departure receipt, current route, selected crew, and bounded objective. Owner events can change the premise. A weather closure, refusal, damaged tool, or message failure becomes an explicit interruption with a safe return or retry route.

### Field 05 expansion — Evidence review state

After return, the player reviews observations one by one. Each observation can be accepted, marked uncertain, linked to a source, or discarded with a reason. Cartography, archive, disaster, and inventory owners receive only accepted facts. The review screen prevents a vivid description from silently becoming a world-state mutation.

### Field 06 expansion — Action state

A reviewed case offers actions that existing owners can execute: update map, request repair, quarantine item, publish warning, propose memorial, schedule follow-up, or close as no action. Every button identifies its owner. A disabled action states whether the problem is missing capability, missing evidence, consent, or timing.

### Field 07 expansion — Stewardship state

A closed action can create a stewardship reminder when an owner returns a maintenance or follow-up event. The reminder keeps the source case and does not become a new damage meter. It can be accepted, deferred, delegated, or archived.

### Field 08 expansion — Reopened state

A case reopens only on a new owner event or an explicit player request. The new delta is shown beside the prior closure. A reopened case does not repay its old reward or duplicate a prior delivery. Its branch graph points back to the original evidence.

### Field 09 expansion — Legacy state

If a package is disabled, a location removed from a content batch, or a save predates a schema field, the case becomes legacy. Legacy preserves source and journal text while offering a base-game route or archive note. It never fabricates a replacement fire mechanic.

### Field 10 expansion — Audited closure

A case reaches audited closure when the owner receipt, player choice, source list, accessibility behavior, save checkpoint, and next review are recorded. The closure can be indexed by location, region, source, survivor, or incident without adding another mutable ledger.

## Pass 58 — Recovery data contract, authoring schema, and migration policy

This pass defines the fields writers and integrators need for high-volume recovery content. It is a proposed content contract, not an implementation claim. The contract is designed to sit beside current JSON authority and require a future accepted loader decision before production use.

### Field 01 expansion — Stable case key

Every row has a snake_case case key scoped to the recovery package. Keys are never derived from display text, timestamps, or hash order. A migration alias can point an old key to a new key, but aliases are immutable once released.

### Field 02 expansion — Owner references

A row names the owner seam for location, route, weather, item, crew, message, archive, consent, and closure. References use canonical IDs or explicit query kinds. A free-text owner name fails validation because it cannot prove reachability.

### Field 03 expansion — Evidence specification

The evidence block defines required sources, confidence labels, timestamps, and acceptable stale age. If a source is unavailable, the row names an authored fallback. The fallback can wait, retry, ask a witness, or close as unknown.

### Field 04 expansion — Action specification

Actions list command ID, owner, prerequisites, success receipt, refusal receipt, timeout, and rollback display. A row may expose several actions, but every action must have a no-op or safe alternative that the player can understand.

### Field 05 expansion — Narrative envelope

Narrative text is separated into title, short summary, long description, speaker lines, uncertainty line, refusal line, closure line, and accessibility label. The envelope records tone, localization context, and maximum panel length. It does not hide gameplay values in string concatenation.

### Field 06 expansion — Privacy envelope

Witness name, likeness, account, and archive destination are individually scoped. A row can require private, household, shelter, regional, or public visibility. The consent owner can narrow scope at runtime; the content row never widens it.

### Field 07 expansion — Save envelope

The row declares which owner receipts make it safe to save, which open fields must restore, and which content version can migrate. It does not define a new save section. A validator rejects a row that claims persistence without naming the current owner.

### Field 08 expansion — Determinism envelope

Seeded variation names its stream purpose, allowed choices, and stable ordering. It cannot use wall-clock time, process identity, or dictionary iteration. A fixture records the seed and expected closure keys.

### Field 09 expansion — Accessibility envelope

Each choice has visible label, disabled reason, focus order, controller action, text equivalent, and quiet-mode policy. Critical notifications point to AudioAccessibilityCoordinator seams. Missing labels fail before a row enters a staged package.

### Field 10 expansion — Migration envelope

A migration row declares old key, new key, preserved receipts, changed copy, fallback behavior, and rollback note. It cannot delete owner state. A disabled package leaves a legacy projection that the archive can still search.

## Pass 59 — Recovery command center UI, focus model, and player comprehension

This pass turns the recovery board into a calm operational workspace. It is a presentation contract over existing data and event seams, not a new gameplay authority.

### Field 01 expansion — Queue overview

The overview shows open, waiting, active, review, stewardship, legacy, and reopened counts as projections. Selecting a count filters the board; it does not change case state. The overview includes a last-updated time and a source-health indicator.

### Field 02 expansion — Evidence column

Each row shows confidence, source type, age, and owner. A player can expand the evidence list to see why the row is reported, observed, or confirmed. The list is paged for large volumes and never loads full narrative detail for every row.

### Field 03 expansion — Next-action panel

The panel places the safest available action first, then alternatives, then a clear disabled explanation. If the action belongs to expedition or inventory, the button opens that owner route with stable context rather than duplicating controls.

### Field 04 expansion — Route preview

A route preview shows canonical region, expected window, closure facts, return condition, and vehicle/crew requirements. It never paints a fire spread overlay that the current owner does not provide. A stale preview is visibly marked.

### Field 05 expansion — Privacy control

A privacy chip shows current consent scope and the owner that can change it. Public, regional, shelter, household, and private views are separate. A player cannot widen a witness record from the recovery panel.

### Field 06 expansion — Review workspace

Returned observations appear as cards with accept, uncertain, link, and discard commands. Keyboard focus follows source order; controller navigation exposes the same choices. The workspace has a text-only mode for low-vision and quiet play.

### Field 07 expansion — Alert center

Critical route, disaster, communications, and return cues appear in a compact alert center with acknowledgment and source. Routine updates coalesce. Visual notices remain available when audio is reduced.

### Field 08 expansion — Archive drawer

The archive drawer shows source chain, correction chain, memorial choice, and retention class. It opens lazily and can be closed without losing the selected recovery row.

### Field 09 expansion — Interruption recovery

If the scene closes, the board reopens to the selected row, restored focus, and last acknowledged alert. A delayed owner event updates the journal once and displays a single reopen cue.

### Field 10 expansion — Error language

Errors use plain language: “The route owner has not confirmed a safe return,” “This account is private,” or “The package is unavailable in this save.” Technical diagnostics remain in development logs.

## Pass 60 — Recovery performance envelope, lifecycle ownership, and stress fixtures

This pass defines bounded performance expectations for high-volume recovery content without prescribing an engine implementation.

### Field 01 expansion — Indexed case list

The list indexes status, region, owner, confidence, age, and privacy scope. Filtering uses metadata and requests detail only for the selected case. A 300-row fixture must not instantiate every narrative node.

### Field 02 expansion — Event subscription budget

Visible boards subscribe to the minimum owner events required by their filters. Hidden panels unsubscribe. A delayed owner event is routed through a central adapter and does not create one subscription per card.

### Field 03 expansion — Archive paging

Archive and source histories are paged by stable cursor. Search results return summaries first, then selected detail. Large source chains do not block the main panel.

### Field 04 expansion — Route refresh cadence

Route and weather refresh on owner event, explicit refresh, or bounded timer. There is no per-frame route query. A stale label tells the player when the last owner response arrived.

### Field 05 expansion — Notification coalescing

Routine observations use the configured coalescing window. Critical disaster and return notifications bypass routine grouping but still use duplicate keys. AudioAccessibilityCoordinator controls ducking and preset behavior.

### Field 06 expansion — Save workload

Recovery captures references and receipts owned elsewhere. Save time grows with open recovery references, not with the total world catalog. A fixture with 100 open references measures serialization and restore separately.

### Field 07 expansion — Memory release

Closing a detail panel releases large narrative, image, and source objects while retaining the selected key. Reopening requests detail again through the adapter.

### Field 08 expansion — Failure isolation

A malformed optional card fails that card or package with a visible diagnostic; it does not prevent base recovery or unrelated owner panels from loading. The fallback preserves the journal entry.

### Field 09 expansion — Deterministic load order

Case indexes, package manifests, and owner event queues use stable ordering. Same-seed stress runs compare selected IDs, receipt order, and closure hashes.

### Field 10 expansion — Stress evidence

Performance evidence records fixture size, active filters, open subscriptions, allocation trend, save duration, restore duration, and observed frame target. A threshold breach produces a bounded follow-up rather than a speculative rewrite.

## Pass 61 — Recovery implementation milestones, ownership gates, and expansion backlog

This pass turns the previous contracts into a dependency-ordered implementation backlog.

### Field 01 expansion — Premise audit

Reconfirm each owner API, data ID, save route, event seam, and UI host immediately before implementation. A stale plan statement is corrected in the ledger before any code change.

### Field 02 expansion — Contract fixture

Add one schema-valid recovery fixture with reported, verified, refused, and closed outcomes. Keep it isolated and focused before adding volume.

### Field 03 expansion — Owner adapter

Implement the thinnest adapter that translates the fixture into current owner commands and receipts. Do not place decisions in the panel.

### Field 04 expansion — Save seam

Wire capture and restore through the existing owner save path for references and receipts. Round-trip the interrupted case before adding more content.

### Field 05 expansion — Accessible slice

Complete one keyboard/controller/text/visual slice before styling the full board. Verify focus restoration after a delayed owner event.

### Field 06 expansion — Determinism slice

Run paired seeded fixtures for selection, assignment, message order, and closure. Remove any accidental wall-clock or unordered variation.

### Field 07 expansion — Content batch

Add a small region batch with 12–24 cards, each carrying owner, fallback, privacy, accessibility, and migration fields.

### Field 08 expansion — Stress batch

Run the bounded 100-, 200-, and 300-card fixtures. Capture evidence and file only the smallest bottleneck repair.

### Field 09 expansion — Rollback rehearsal

Disable the package against a fixture save with open cards, confirm legacy projection, then restore the package and verify stable reconnection.

### Field 10 expansion — Handoff gate

Hand off only the fixture results, touched paths, untouched shared paths, limitations, and next bounded package. Do not claim the entire recovery system is integrated.

## Pass 62 — Recovery governance, player-facing explanations, and long-horizon content health

This pass adds governance rules for the period after the first recovery slice ships.

### Field 01 expansion — Evidence freshness

Every open card states its freshness class and the event that can invalidate it. A player can request refresh, accept the stale risk where permitted, or defer.

### Field 02 expansion — Source disagreement

Conflicting reports remain linked and visible. The recovery board offers compare, verify, or proceed with safe unknown; it never hides the lower-confidence source.

### Field 03 expansion — Survivor dignity

Witnesses can decline, correct, pause, or withdraw an account. The journal records the boundary and avoids using refusal as a punitive branch.

### Field 04 expansion — Regional fairness

Remote shelters receive the same explanation of route, supply, and consent requirements even when their available actions differ. Differences come from owner evidence, not arbitrary content gating.

### Field 05 expansion — Archive stewardship

Public records include source and correction links. Private records remain discoverable only through the owner-approved path.

### Field 06 expansion — Seasonal review

At each winter phase or season change, open cards are re-evaluated only when an owner event makes the premise relevant. The board explains the changed window.

### Field 07 expansion — Content retirement

Retired cards leave a searchable legacy note and preserve completed receipts. They do not leave dangling buttons or erase a player’s journal.

### Field 08 expansion — Writer feedback

Production diagnostics identify cards with repeated fallback, excessive owner timeout, inaccessible wording, or low closure rate. Writers revise the card contract rather than adding more branches blindly.

### Field 09 expansion — Release notes

Each batch lists new owner seams, supported records, known gaps, migration behavior, and player-visible changes. Release language stays within StoreCapabilityManifest evidence.

### Field 10 expansion — Long-horizon review

A quarterly review samples active, closed, reopened, legacy, and private cards. The sample verifies continuity, performance, privacy, accessibility, and deterministic replay.

### Pass 62 governance acceptance

Recovery content remains healthy when new volume increases playable choices without increasing hidden state, duplicate ownership, inaccessible decisions, or untraceable claims. Governance reviews keep the wave expandable while preserving a clear boundary around what is implemented and what remains a proposal.

## Pass 63 — Seasonal recovery economy and phase-aware field planning

This pass uses NuclearWinterProgressionSystem and WeatherGameplayCascade outputs to make recovery timing meaningful without creating a new ecology or fire-spread authority.

### Field 01 — Phase briefing
The briefing names current phase, season, temperature, daylight, heating pressure, expedition window, greenhouse condition, and anomaly notes from existing owners. Recovery content interprets those facts but never changes them.

### Field 02 — Work-window choice
A card can recommend dawn, daylight, thaw, calm wind, or sheltered work. Expedition and weather owners confirm the actual window; a recommendation remains reversible until departure.

### Field 03 — Fuel and shelter request
Field teams can request fuel, shelter, food, or rest through inventory, colony, vehicle, and needs owners. Recovery shows shortages and safe alternatives without creating a recovery ration ledger.

### Field 04 — Seasonal evidence
Ash drift, meltwater, frost cracks, and green return are observations tagged with season and source. Agriculture, water, shelter, and archive owners decide their operational meaning.

### Field 05 — Route adaptation
A seasonal closure can redirect a case to a tunnel, relay, outpost, or later window. Cartography and expedition owners supply route truth; recovery records the decision and reason.

### Field 06 — Survivor pacing
Needs, health, autonomy, and roster owners can return rest, refusal, substitution, or limited assignment. The content does not translate phase into hidden fatigue points.

### Field 07 — Community timing
A seasonal recovery notice can align with a holiday, memorial, or work meeting. SeasonalCelebrationSystem and communications owners provide the context and record.

### Field 08 — Greenhouse handoff
A burn-scar garden request asks agriculture or greenhouse owners for readiness, seed, water, and labor. The story can celebrate a plan without claiming a harvest.

### Field 09 — Seasonal reopen
A phase transition reopens only cards whose owner premise changed. The board states the changed fact and does not flood the player with every historical card.

### Field 10 — Phase closure
A seasonal review closes with evidence, action, and next window. The review is archived with source and phase, not stored as a second seasonal system.

## Pass 64 — Recovery camp logistics, return assurance, and supply-chain handoff

This pass expands temporary field operations through vehicle, expedition, inventory, colony, communications, and archive owners.

### Field 01 — Camp request
A camp request names canonical site, crew, vehicle capability, rest requirement, cargo, signal route, and closure condition. Recovery does not create a camp inventory.

### Field 02 — Pack list
Inventory returns actual item IDs, quantities, reservations, and condition. The pack list explains missing and substituted items.

### Field 03 — Departure assurance
Expedition and vehicle owners return route, departure, return, and cargo facts. A departure button is disabled until the required receipt exists.

### Field 04 — Camp status
Status is projected as proposed, accepted, active, packing, returning, or unresolved from owner receipts. Recovery stores references, not a camp simulation.

### Field 05 — Signal plan
Communications provides frequency, range, acknowledgment, jamming, and retry. The field card includes a low-signal fallback such as courier or scheduled return.

### Field 06 — Rest and care
Needs, health, medical, and shelter owners can require rest, care, or early return. The panel explains the owner constraint without inventing a camp fatigue number.

### Field 07 — Sample custody
A sample handoff names collector, source, container, time, and destination owner. Inventory or laboratory owner confirms receipt; recovery never assumes delivery.

### Field 08 — Pack failure
A failed packing operation states missing item, damaged item, route closure, or crew refusal. The player can repair, substitute, defer, or abandon with a receipt.

### Field 09 — Return proof
Return requires vehicle/expedition receipt, cargo reconciliation, crew status, and open-question list. A silent return cannot close the case.

### Field 10 — Camp archive
The archive receives camp source, map, samples, witness accounts, and unresolved questions under consent and retention rules.

## Pass 65 — Terrain observation, wildlife coexistence, and noncombat recovery choices

This pass adds terrain and wildlife flavor using current observation, quota, conflict, taming, cartography, and expedition projections. It does not add fire-caused ecology or a wildlife simulation.

### Field 01 — Observation purpose
Every encounter states whether it is map, safety, habitat, quota, conflict, or memory work. The purpose chooses the existing owner query.

### Field 02 — Distance choice
Players can observe, avoid, reroute, wait, or request a specialist. Wildlife and expedition owners decide the result.

### Field 03 — Evidence quality
Tracks, calls, damaged fencing, and sightings are reported or observed with source and time. A vivid line is not a confirmed population change.

### Field 04 — Quota boundary
A quota or conflict result is received from the current wildlife owner. Recovery can connect a report to it but cannot create a quota counter.

### Field 05 — Taming boundary
A taming or companionship outcome comes from the existing taming owner. Recovery stories may show relationship consequences only through survivor or animal receipts.

### Field 06 — Route safety
Cartography and expedition decide whether a route is open, narrow, delayed, or unsafe. No wildlife card opens a route.

### Field 07 — Community response
A shelter can choose warning, escort, observation, or quiet coexistence through communications and colony owners.

### Field 08 — Archive choice
Wildlife observations can remain private field notes, map annotations, public warnings, or research sources.

### Field 09 — Repeated encounter
Cadence keys suppress duplicate observations while allowing a new owner event or season to reopen the thread.

### Field 10 — Closure
A terrain encounter closes with a safe player decision, owner result, source, and next route.

## Pass 91–97 — Recovery operations packet

The fire recovery proposal keeps ecological change, shelter needs, travel risk, and survivor memory connected through existing authorities. Each packet is optional content until an owner receipt proves that the route, persistence, and player-facing consequence already have a safe seam. The following fields are deliberately concrete enough for a builder to claim, but each field remains subject to current-source verification.

### Pass 91 — Ember Weather Windows

#### Field 1 — Authority Seam

The slice is introduced as a bounded expansion that can stand beside current content. For **ember weather windows**, the authority seam field must identify the existing owner, event route, and save boundary before any field is added. The data authority supplies identifiers and authored values, while the current runtime owner validates and applies them. Events should expose facts for UI and narrative subscribers, with save capture and restore remaining on the established path. If the current seam cannot carry the field, the plan stops at a documented blocker and requests an architecture decision. The review record should explain which assumption was verified, which evidence was unavailable, and which follow-up remains outside this package.

#### Field 2 — Player Loop

The design starts from a player-observable need and traces it back to one authoritative seam. For **ember weather windows**, the player loop field must describe the smallest playable loop, its inputs, its outputs, and the feedback the player receives. The loop should remain legible during pressure: the player can inspect the cause, decide, act, and understand why the outcome changed. The content supports short sessions and return visits by exposing progress, interruption state, and the next useful action. The player receives a clear prompt, chooses among bounded actions, sees immediate feedback, and later sees the consequence in the world. The review record should explain which assumption was verified, which evidence was unavailable, and which follow-up remains outside this package.

The implementation brief records the smallest version that can be reviewed before wider content is authored. For **ember weather windows**, the data packet field must define authored identifiers, ranges, references, migration rules, and catalog validation expectations. The packet keeps mutable state out of panels and caches, preserving the current owner for inventory, needs, health, travel, and campaign facts. Authored records use stable snake_case identifiers, explicit schema versions, bounded ranges, and references that the integrity validator can explain. Migration records must state whether an old value is mapped, defaulted, archived, or rejected, with deterministic ordering for every conversion. The review record should explain which assumption was verified, which evidence was unavailable, and which follow-up remains outside this package.

The field begins with a premise audit and a named owner receipt. For **ember weather windows**, the state ladder field must map entry, active, interrupted, recovered, expired, and replay states with deterministic transitions. The state ladder covers normal completion, interruption, abandonment, recovery, and replay without silently duplicating rewards or penalties. Every transition has an initiating fact, an allowed caller, a deterministic outcome, and a persistence expectation that can be tested independently. Interrupted work remains inspectable and resumes through the same owner rather than a second shadow ledger. ## Pass 98 — Fields 11–20 after the 100k gate

Crossing the first volume gate adds a second field layer to the recovery packet. These fields extend each recovery slice with provenance, policy, tooling, observability, and long-tail content. They do not create a second fire authority. Each field must resolve through the current owner, and each implementation claim remains conditional on a current premise audit.

### Field 11 — Evidence provenance

Every burn scar, smoke report, and regrowth marker needs a source label that tells the player and the reviewer where the fact came from. A source can be a scout observation, a shelter report, a deterministic simulation result, or an authored historical record. The label is presentation metadata; the authoritative fact remains in the existing world, travel, needs, or campaign owner. Provenance records must survive a save round trip when the underlying fact survives, and they must disappear cleanly when a temporary observation expires. A focused fixture should compare source labels across two same-seed runs and confirm that no iteration order changes the displayed history.

### Field 12 — Recovery policy cards

Policy cards describe the limits of a recovery action before the player commits. One card can state a work-hour limit, a smoke threshold, a protected habitat rule, or a consent requirement for entering a memorial site. Cards are authored data, not executable policy hidden in a panel. The host can explain a card and route a command, while Core checks the rule against current state. The card format needs a stable ID, a short title, a long explanation, a severity, a prerequisite, and a failure message. Migration must preserve old records by mapping absent fields to explicit safe defaults.

### Field 13 — Field notebook tooling

The recovery notebook gives scouts a reviewable way to collect observations without becoming a second ledger. A notebook entry stores the observation ID, location reference, timestamp from the deterministic session clock, confidence, and optional witness reference. It can point to an existing fire, route, or settlement fact, but it cannot invent a new hazard through text entry. The UI needs filters for unreviewed, confirmed, contradicted, and archived entries. A reviewer command either promotes the observation through the established owner or leaves it as evidence only. Save tests must prove that a partially written notebook cannot duplicate a promoted fact.

### Field 14 — Seasonal policy rotation

Recovery rules change with rain, wind, frost, and planting windows. Seasonal rotation is represented as an authored schedule consumed by the existing calendar owner. It should expose the active policy ID and the next transition time as facts. The runtime must not recalculate a policy from wall-clock time or local machine culture. When a save is restored across a season boundary, the owner recomputes the active schedule from the saved deterministic clock, then emits one refresh event. The panel shows the current and upcoming rule, while the plan records how old saves remain legible when a policy was retired.

### Field 15 — Community consent log

Some recovery work touches graves, sacred trees, private caches, or locations with contested ownership. A consent log records who granted access, what scope was granted, the expiry condition, and the consequence of violating the agreement. It is a campaign or relationship fact only when the current owner already models that relationship; otherwise it remains an authored prompt awaiting an architecture decision. The log must support withdrawal and renegotiation without erasing history. UI copy distinguishes a request, a granted permission, and a completed action, so a player never mistakes dialogue selection for completed consent.

### Field 16 — Long-tail regrowth content

After a firebreak is finished, the space should continue to produce small observations and choices. Long-tail content includes returning birds, invasive shoots, washed-out markers, volunteer fatigue, and an unexpected safe route. Each entry references an existing location and reward owner, has a bounded repeat policy, and declares whether it is once-only, seasonal, or replayable. The authoring table includes a quiet version for players who prefer low interruption. Content review checks that a long-tail entry adds a new decision or interpretation rather than repeating an earlier line with a different noun.

### Field 17 — Recovery telemetry

Telemetry is limited to facts useful for balancing and debugging: time spent in a recovery state, abandoned actions, blocked commands, save size, event fan-out, and panel refresh count. It must not collect private free text or hidden player identity. The event names and sampling policy live beside the owning seam, and disabled telemetry leaves gameplay unchanged. A focused fixture records a bounded session with telemetry on and off, then compares state hashes. Any difference is a release blocker because observability must remain a read-only consumer of recovery facts.

### Field 18 — Heat and smoke accessibility mode

The plan adds an accessibility option that replaces rapidly changing heat and smoke cues with persistent status text, icon shape, and an inspectable timeline. The mode affects presentation timing and visual emphasis only; the hazard calculation stays in the existing needs or environment authority. The panel explains whether the change is cosmetic or changes a permitted timing window. Controller users can open the same status detail without a pointer. Acceptance includes high contrast, reduced motion, keyboard-only navigation, and a localized string fixture with long hazard names.

### Field 19 — Recovery archive export

At a campaign endpoint, the player can review a compact archive of scars, repaired routes, memorial choices, and unresolved observations. The archive is generated from current facts in stable ordering and can be read after a reload. It is not a new save store and does not become a dependency for active play. If export is implemented, the format must be versioned, omit secrets and private notes, and fail with a visible message when a referenced record is unavailable. The acceptance receipt includes a sample archive, a missing-reference fixture, and a checksum comparison for two identical seeds.

### Field 20 — Recovery handoff matrix

The integrator receives a matrix linking every recovery field to its owner, data record, event, save section, UI route, focused test, and known blocker. A blank cell is meaningful: it says the field is still design-only or requires a signed architecture decision. The matrix is reviewed after each implementation slice and archived with the handoff. It prevents prose growth from being mistaken for integration and gives future turns a safe starting point. The field closes only when current source, runtime evidence, and rollback instructions agree.

For **charcoal road inventories**, the authority seam field must verify the current owner, command route, event boundary, and save section before implementation. Events expose facts to panels and narrative consumers without granting subscribers mutation rights. The host presents facts while Core validates commands and owns durable state. An unproven seam becomes a documented blocker and architecture decision rather than a new registry. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 2 — Player Loop

Trace the player-visible question through data, runtime, save, UI, and narrative seams. For **charcoal road inventories**, the player loop field must define entry, choice, cost, feedback, interruption, and the next useful action. A failure explains cause and recovery while preventing duplicate rewards or silent penalties. Return visits reveal progress, interruption, unresolved risk, and a useful next action in stable status language. The player sees a clear prompt, chooses among bounded options, receives feedback, and can inspect a later consequence. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 3 — Data Contract

Describe the smallest reviewable version before high-volume content or prose is added. For **charcoal road inventories**, the data contract field must define stable IDs, schema version, ranges, references, migration, and validator diagnostics. Records use snake_case IDs, explicit versions, bounded values, resolvable references, and diagnostic failures. Authoring tools show required fields, examples, dependencies, and repair guidance before runtime loading. Migration notes state whether old fields are mapped, defaulted, archived, or rejected. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 4 — State Ladder

Start with a current-source premise receipt and a bounded implementation claim. For **charcoal road inventories**, the state ladder field must map pending, active, paused, complete, failed, expired, and replay transitions deterministically. Interrupted work remains visible and resumes through the same authority with duplicate completion fixtures. Replay policy distinguishes resettable content from one-time history with retained completion evidence. Expiry communicates cause, keeps useful history, and leaves a follow-up route when appropriate. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 5 — Interface Route

Frame the topic as a playable expansion whose facts remain with existing owners. For **charcoal road inventories**, the interface route field must define panel hierarchy, detail view, focus order, commands, empty states, and refresh source. Keyboard, controller, and pointer inputs share a route and restore previous focus on close. The interface reads status, next action, consequence, and reason text from authoritative facts. Markers and journals reinforce outcomes without becoming a second gameplay authority. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 6 — Accessibility

Trace the player-visible question through data, runtime, save, UI, and narrative seams. For **charcoal road inventories**, the accessibility field must cover readable terms, contrast, text scale, remapping, reduced motion, and invalid-input recovery. Fixtures cover controller-only, keyboard-only, long localization, and narrow layouts. Contrast, focus, scaling, remapping, reduced motion, and non-timed alternatives are acceptance requirements. Copy uses stable terms, avoids unexplained abbreviations, and allows time to inspect consequential choices. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 7 — Performance

Describe the smallest reviewable version before high-volume content or prose is added. For **charcoal road inventories**, the performance field must set work budgets, batching, cache ownership, lazy loading, allocation targets, and degradation. The budget states frequency, worst-case record count, safe degradation, and proving metric. Batching and lazy loading protect scene entry and refresh cost while preserving seeded results. Caches have one owner, explicit invalidation, bounded lifetime, and deterministic ordering. The review receipt records owner evidence, data and runtime observations, focused verification, accessibility checks, and the follow-up outside this package.

#### Field 8 — Content Bank

Start with a current-source premise receipt and a bounded implementation claim. For **charcoal road inventories**, the content bank field must author tasks, voices, locations, encounters, rewards, consequences, and follow-up hooks. Side content adds a new decision or interpretation instead of renaming a main objective. The table records tone, pacing, prerequisites, failure text, repeat policy, and expected outcome. Characters have boundaries and motivations while rewards route through existing owners. #### Field 10 — Rollout

## Wave 35 integration closeout receipt — Plan 1: Wildland Firefronts and Burn Recovery

**Closeout status:** documentation-only; READY FOR PREMISE AUDIT. This receipt does not claim implementation.

**Program role:** wildland fire, burn recovery, weather cascade, disaster response, expedition, vehicle, wildlife, communications, cartography, and archive

**Primary owners:** weather cascade, shelter fire, disaster response, expedition, vehicle, wildlife, communications, cartography, and archive owners

**Required delta:** a provenance-aware recovery command that can inspect an existing hazard or weather fact, choose a bounded response, and show a later recovery consequence without inventing a second fire, ecology, route, or inventory ledger

**First safe slice:** one smoke-observation report linked to an existing weather or expedition result, with inspect, defer, share, refuse, and recovery callback outcomes

**Evidence anchors:** ash creek markers, a charred gate hinge, a wet seed pouch, and a radio note folded into a map

**Observable signals:** smoke age, burn confidence, route closure, seed viability, crew fatigue, and recovery callback

### Closeout boundary

The plan closes at the design boundary where one current owner can publish a fact, one consumer can display or consume it, one command can be issued through the owner, and one recovery path can return the player to a known state. The plan does not create a second ledger, registry, cache authority, save store, event bus, or presentation-owned counter. A row remains design-only until a current source search proves its consumer.

### Integration contract

The first receipt must identify the owner, public API, data file, save section or stateless proof, host route, focused tests, and rollback. It must exercise source age, stale input, duplicate delivery, interruption, correction, keyboard/controller parity, empty and error states, and one delayed content callback. The same seed and ordered inputs must reproduce the result across save, reload, host reopen, and duplicate event delivery.

### Content and failure gate

The first content slice uses field reports, ashline witnesses, seed-bank visits, evacuee promises, return-route complications, and archive entries. It includes discovery, interpretation, complication, competing interest, choice, quiet success, costly success, refusal, unresolved outcome, delayed callback, repeat policy, and retirement rule. It must stop safely for duplicate hazard state, speculative fire spread, unsafe wildlife mutation, route truth drift, and unbounded event fan-out. Prose can describe evidence and uncertainty but cannot create a gameplay fact.

### Handoff

**MUST PRESERVE:** existing authority, engine-free Core, JSON data authority, deterministic ordering, current save ownership, truthful UI, and active path claims.

**MUST ADD:** one premise receipt, one owner-bound slice, one validator-backed sample, one replay or stateless proof, one accessible route, one focused verification result, and one rollback note.

**MUST NOT DO:** duplicate state, revive retired architecture, claim runtime integration from document volume, or widen the catalog before reachability.

**NEXT ACTION:** run the bounded premise audit for the first safe slice and return the evidence to the integrator.
